Day 53 of 100 · Networking Deep Dive

TCP vs UDP

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityNetworking Deep DivePublished artifact recovered

TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream; UDP provides independent best-effort datagrams with lower protocol overhead and different application responsibilities.

Architecture / mental model

TCP: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK → ordered byte stream
UDP: application datagram → best-effort delivery

How it works

TCP is connection-oriented and tracks sequence, acknowledgement, retransmission, flow control and congestion control. Applications receive a byte stream rather than preserved message boundaries.

UDP is connectionless at the transport layer: there is no built-in delivery, ordering or retransmission guarantee, and datagram boundaries are preserved.

Protocol choice is not simply 'reliable versus fast.' Applications such as QUIC build sophisticated reliability and congestion behavior above UDP because UDP gives them different control over transport semantics.

Hands-on reference

ss -lntup
nc -vz HOST 443
sudo tcpdump -ni any 'tcp port 443 or udp port 53'

Verification

Capture a TCP connection and identify SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK; compare with a UDP DNS exchange and observe the lack of a TCP-style connection handshake.

Field note / gotcha

TCP is a byte stream. One sender `send()` does not guarantee one receiver `recv()` with the same message boundary.

Security considerations

Both protocols need explicit firewall policy and application validation. UDP spoofing/amplification risks and long-lived TCP resource usage create different attack surfaces.

What I learned

Transport semantics determine what reliability work the application can assume and what it must provide itself.
